Apify rotates API tokens, prompts 2FA resets after breach

Apify disclosed unauthorized access to parts of its internal systems on November 9–10, prompting it to rotate API tokens and proxy passwords, reset active sessions, and revoke some OAuth integrations. The company says it found no evidence that customer account data was affected, but some users must reset 2FA because their codes may have been exposed.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Apify said an unauthorized third party accessed parts of its internal systems on November 9 and 10, 2026, and the company detected the incident on November 11 at 12:13 UTC.
  • 02Apify responded by cutting off the attacker’s access, invalidating internal credentials, rotating API tokens, and resetting all active sessions.
  • 03The company revoked OAuth connections to external integrations, including GitHub, and said affected users would be notified by email when it is safe to reconnect.
  • 04Apify said it found no indication that account data stored on its platform was affected, while impacted customers’ Apify API tokens and Apify Proxy passwords were rotated.
  • 05Some affected customers were advised to reset two-factor authentication through the Apify Console because their two-factor authentication codes may have been exposed, although Apify said passwords remained safe.

Apify disclosed that an unauthorized third party accessed parts of its internal systems on November 9 and 10, 2026. The company detected the activity on November 11 at 12:13 UTC, cut off the attacker’s access, and began an investigation into the impact. Apify is a Czech web-scraping and browser-automation platform that reports having 80,000 customers.

In response, Apify invalidated internal credentials, rotated API tokens and Apify Proxy passwords for impacted customers, and reset all active sessions. It also revoked OAuth connections to external services, including GitHub, and said affected users would receive email when it is safe to reconnect. Apify said it found no indication that account data stored on its platform was affected, but advised some customers to reset two-factor authentication because their codes may have been exposed, while stating that passwords remain safe.

  • The incident response treated access credentials and connected third-party accounts as separate risks: Apify rotated API and proxy credentials while also revoking OAuth links such as GitHub connections.
  • Affected users may need to reset two-factor authentication even though Apify said passwords remained safe, because the company warned that two-factor codes may have been exposed.
  • Apify revoked external OAuth connections as a precaution and plans to notify affected users by email when reconnection is safe, rather than asking them to reconnect immediately.
  • Although Apify reported no indication that stored account data was affected, it still reset all active sessions and rotated customer-facing access credentials.

Apify, a Czech company whose service helps businesses collect data from websites and social media, says an outside party accessed parts of its internal systems on November 9 and 10. The company reset sign-ins, changed customer access keys and proxy passwords, and disconnected some links to outside services such as GitHub. It says it has found no sign that customer data stored on its platform was affected, but some customers must reset their two-step sign-in codes because those codes may have been exposed. This matters because Apify serves about 80,000 customers, so stolen access details could otherwise let someone use customer accounts or connected services without permission.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Apify reported unauthorized access to internal systems and rotated affected API tokens, proxy passwords, sessions, and OAuth connections. Security professionals using Apify or connected GitHub integrations should review the incident because exposed access credentials and 2FA codes may affect customers.

Your Endpoint Management Platform Could Be Your Biggest Security Risk

Sponsored by Action1, the article argues that endpoint-management platforms are high-value compromise points because attackers can abuse their trusted administrative access at scale. It promotes customer-controlled cryptographic authorization, via Action1 Endpoint Takeover Prevention, as a safeguard for high-risk endpoint actions even if the management platform is compromised.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Endpoint management platforms can deploy patches, install software, run scripts, enforce configurations, and remotely manage large numbers of devices from a central system.
  • 02The article cites incidents involving BeyondTrust Bomgar, SimpleHelp, ConnectWise ScreenConnect, and Microsoft Intune in which compromised or abused management infrastructure was used to access systems, deploy ransomware, steal information, or wipe devices.
  • 03The article states that multi-factor authentication, access controls, privileged-access management, and activity monitoring operate primarily within a management platform’s own security boundaries.
  • 04Action1 says its Endpoint Takeover Prevention requires sensitive actions such as script execution, software deployment, automations, and remote sessions to be approved with a customer-controlled cryptographic key.
  • 05The article notes that this approach depends on secure key management, endpoint integrity, and proper configuration of protected operations.

Endpoint management platforms give administrators centralized ability to patch devices, install software, execute scripts, enforce configurations, and provide remote management. The article warns that these same trusted channels and elevated permissions make such platforms attractive targets, because an attacker who gains control can issue commands, distribute malware, disable security controls, or disrupt operations across many endpoints. It cites cases involving BeyondTrust Bomgar, SimpleHelp, ConnectWise ScreenConnect, and Microsoft Intune in which management infrastructure was compromised or abused to access systems, steal information, deploy ransomware, or wipe devices.

The article argues that controls such as multi-factor authentication, role-based access, privileged-access management, and activity monitoring may not independently establish whether a sensitive endpoint command was approved by a legitimate administrator. It promotes customer-controlled cryptographic authorization, in which an endpoint verifies a command approval signed with a private key held separately from the management platform. Action1 presents its Endpoint Takeover Prevention as applying this approach to script execution, software deployment, automations, and remote sessions, while noting that secure key management, endpoint integrity, and proper configuration remain necessary.

  • A management platform’s normal, approved connections and elevated permissions can make malicious commands appear legitimate to the devices it manages after the platform is compromised.
  • Controls such as multi-factor authentication and role-based permissions may not independently prove that a sensitive command was approved by a real administrator if an attacker hijacks an authenticated session or privileged service.
  • Keeping the private approval key outside the management platform means compromising the platform alone should not let an attacker authorize protected actions.
  • For cloud-hosted management services, a compromise of the provider’s hosting, management, or software-delivery systems may affect multiple customer environments at once.
  • The article emphasizes that independent authorization still relies on customers securely managing their keys, preserving device integrity, and correctly choosing which actions require protection.

The article warns that the central tools companies use to update, control, and support many work computers can become dangerous if criminals take them over. It cites cases involving BeyondTrust Bomgar, SimpleHelp, ConnectWise ScreenConnect, and Microsoft Intune, where attackers used trusted management access to reach customers’ systems, steal information, install ransomware, or erase devices. This matters because one compromised management service can give an attacker broad control over an entire organization, or even several organizations. The sponsored article promotes Action1’s approach of requiring a separate customer-held digital approval before especially risky actions can run.

Microsoft confirms Windows security updates installation issues

Microsoft confirmed that November 2026 Windows 11 security update KB5132061 can fail on some devices that installed the October preview update KB5127936, producing installation errors. Microsoft says an automatic repair will reach affected devices within 24–48 hours, after which the security update should install normally.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft confirmed that some Windows 11 devices cannot complete installation of the November 2026 security update KB5132061.
  • 02The issue affects a limited number of devices that installed the October 2026 non-security preview update KB5127936, while devices that did not install that preview update are not affected.
  • 03Affected devices may repeatedly attempt the update or display error codes 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993.
  • 04Microsoft said it will automatically repair affected devices within 24 to 48 hours from November 11, 2026, after which Windows Update will download and install the November security update.
  • 05Microsoft advised IT administrators to contact Microsoft Support if installation issues continue after 48 hours.

Microsoft confirmed that the November 2026 Windows 11 security update, KB5132061, may fail to install on a limited number of devices. The problem affects systems that previously installed the October 2026 non-security preview update, KB5127936. Devices that did not receive the October preview update are not affected, according to Microsoft.

Affected systems may repeatedly try to install the update, freeze partway through installation, or show error codes 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993. Microsoft said it will automatically repair affected devices within 24 to 48 hours starting November 11, 2026, after which Windows Update should download and install the November security update. The company said end users do not need to take action and advised IT administrators to contact Microsoft Support if the issue persists after 48 hours.

  • The installation problem is narrowly linked to devices that installed the October 2026 optional preview update, rather than to all Windows 11 systems receiving the November security update.
  • Microsoft expects the repair to occur automatically, so affected end users do not need to manually fix their computers before the security update can be installed.
  • The issue can present as repeated update attempts as well as several different error codes, which may make the same underlying problem appear differently across affected devices.
  • IT administrators should wait through Microsoft's stated 24-to-48-hour repair window and contact Microsoft Support only if affected devices still fail afterward.

Microsoft says some Windows 11 computers cannot install its November 2026 security update if they previously installed an optional October update. These computers may get stuck while updating or show error messages, but Microsoft says it will automatically repair the problem within 24 to 48 hours and then install the security update. This matters because security updates help protect computers, and installation failures can leave affected users waiting longer for those protections.

Hackers compromise 4,800 GitHub accounts to steal cloud credentials

The wfx-loot campaign used 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 repositories and inject credential-stealing GitHub Actions workflows, stealing secrets from at least 1,835 targets. Affected repository owners should investigate suspicious pull requests and workflow changes and immediately rotate all workflow-accessible secrets and cloud credentials.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The wfx-loot campaign used credentials from 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts to probe 61,764 repositories for write access beginning around 12:45 UTC on November 10.
  • 02The attackers opened pull requests titled “docs: dependency audit notes” and injected a 1,500-line script into GitHub Actions workflows, short-lived branches, or npm install hooks to steal credentials.
  • 03Researchers confirmed that secrets were stolen from at least 1,835 targets, although not every targeted repository ran the malicious payload.
  • 04The script targeted GitHub Actions tokens, AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credentials, developer keys, package-registry credentials, and credentials for AI services and developer tools.
  • 05Repository owners are advised to search for the “wfx-docs” branch, the suspicious pull request, and gaps in workflow run numbers, and to rotate all secrets and cloud roles available to affected workflows.

The wfx-loot campaign targeted tens of thousands of GitHub repositories using credentials from 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts. Beginning around 12:45 UTC on November 10, the attacker probed 61,764 repositories for write access by opening pull requests titled “docs: dependency audit notes.” Researchers confirmed that secrets were stolen from at least 1,835 targets. Some compromised accounts were associated with Fortune 100 organizations, the U.S. General Services Administration, the French government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO.

The attacker delivered a 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script through modified GitHub Actions workflows, new workflows on short-lived branches, or npm install hooks. It sought GitHub Actions tokens, AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credentials, developer and infrastructure keys, package-registry credentials, AI service credentials, and secrets from files, shell histories, process memory, commits, and workflow artifacts. The script could exchange GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary cloud sessions and, where permitted, create long-lived credentials or alter cloud identity and trust policies. The attacker reverted changes and deleted workflow runs and logs in under a minute, and affected repository owners are advised to investigate the “wfx-docs” branch, suspicious pull requests, and workflow-run gaps before rotating exposed secrets and cloud roles.

  • About 92% of the malicious pull requests remained open, indicating that many repository owners had not noticed the probing activity.
  • The attackers could erase workflow runs and logs and revert their changes in under a minute, making the activity harder to detect after execution.
  • Roughly 50 compromised accounts appeared to have publishing rights on package ecosystems, and automated publishing placed the payload in one Packagist package release and two Go module versions.
  • The stolen GitHub identity tokens could be exchanged for temporary cloud sessions and, where permissions allowed, used to create long-lived credentials or change cloud trust policies for persistent access.

Hackers used thousands of stolen GitHub accounts to make seemingly ordinary code-change requests in more than 61,000 software projects, then added hidden instructions that copied passwords, access keys, and cloud account information. At least 1,835 projects had secrets stolen, and affected accounts included ones tied to major companies, U.S. and French government organizations, and open-source projects. This matters because those stolen keys can let criminals enter other online services, take further control of cloud accounts, or create lasting access even after the original code changes are removed.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a high-impact supply-chain incident involving thousands of compromised GitHub accounts, more than 61,000 probed repositories, and confirmed secret theft from at least 1,835 targets. It is immediately actionable because affected workflow credentials and cloud roles should be treated as compromised and rotated.

New Windows SignDrop zero-day gives hackers SYSTEM privileges

Researcher Abdelhamid Naceri released SignDrop, an unpatched Windows zero-day that abuses CLFS authentication-file handling to potentially elevate local privileges to SYSTEM and bypass antimalware tamper protection on many Windows systems.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri released SignDrop, a Windows zero-day proof of concept that can grant SYSTEM-level privileges by abusing CLFS authentication-file creation.
  • 02The flaw stems from CLFS logic that can create an authentication file with SYSTEM privileges when a privileged process, such as Windows Defender, later opens a log file.
  • 03Naceri said the technique can bypass antimalware self-defense because arbitrary file creation can appear to originate from the antimalware product’s legitimate process.
  • 04Naceri tested SignDrop on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, and estimated that 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable.
  • 05There is currently no solution other than waiting for a Microsoft patch, because disabling the CLFS mitigation would expose devices to memory-corruption attacks.

Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri, also known as Nightmare Eclipse, released SignDrop, a Windows zero-day proof of concept that can give attackers SYSTEM-level privileges. The flaw affects the Common Log File System (CLFS) driver’s handling of authentication files created for new log files. Naceri said it abuses a Microsoft mitigation introduced in October 2025 to defend against authentication attacks targeting CLFS vulnerabilities.

According to Naceri, CLFS performs access checks correctly when a log file is created, but its logic can be abused when a privileged process later opens that file. Processes such as Windows Defender can be forced to open the files, causing an authentication file to be created with SYSTEM privileges and the original file’s permissions. Naceri said this can bypass antimalware tamper protection because the file-creation request appears to come from the antimalware process itself.

Naceri tested SignDrop on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, and estimated that 80% of Windows installations are vulnerable. He said systems can be checked with the proof of concept or by examining the CLFS Authentication Mode registry value, where values of 0 or 1 indicate vulnerability. There is currently no solution other than waiting for a Microsoft patch, since disabling the CLFS mitigation would expose devices to memory-corruption attacks.

  • A Microsoft mitigation introduced in October 2025 to reduce CLFS-related authentication attacks is itself the condition that enables SignDrop’s abuse path.
  • A device can be checked for exposure by running the proof of concept or inspecting the CLFS Authentication\Mode registry value; values of 0 or 1 indicate vulnerability according to Naceri.
  • The technique can cause a privileged process such as Windows Defender to create files under its own identity, which Naceri said allows it to bypass the self-protection mechanisms of antimalware products.
  • Disabling the CLFS mitigation is not presented as a safe workaround because it would reopen systems to attacks using CLFS memory-corruption flaws.

A security researcher released SignDrop, a newly discovered Windows flaw that could let someone who already has access to a computer gain the system’s highest level of control. It may affect an estimated 80% of Windows installations, including tested versions of Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025. The flaw can also be used to weaken or turn off security software, and there is currently no fix from Microsoft; disabling the affected Windows protection could expose computers to other known weaknesses.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports a newly released, unpatched Windows privilege-escalation proof of concept that could affect a large share of installations and may bypass antimalware tamper protections. Although the article does not report active exploitation, the potential for SYSTEM-level access and lack of a safe workaround make it broadly relevant.

Hackers plant GSocket on Linux servers for persistent access

Threat actors are increasingly using the legitimate GSocket remote-access tool to persist on compromised Linux web and hosting servers through outbound encrypted relay connections that bypass inbound firewall controls. Defenders should remove GSocket artifacts, audit persistence mechanisms, restrict egress traffic, and patch exposed systems.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Multiple threat actors are abusing the legitimate open-source GSocket remote-access tool to retain access to Linux servers after the initial vulnerabilities used to compromise them are patched.
  • 02Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry recorded a 356.2% increase in GSocket-related detections between March and August.
  • 03GSocket routes encrypted sessions through its Global Socket Relay Network, allowing both the compromised host and attacker to connect outward without requiring an inbound listener or public server address.
  • 04Of detected GSocket incidents, 87.1% involved web applications and hosting environments, with PHP applications and cPanel hosting accounting for 63.9% and Apache for 24.3%.
  • 05Researchers observed attackers using cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files to make GSocket persist on compromised hosts.

Multiple threat actors are abusing GSocket, a legitimate open-source remote-access tool, to maintain access to compromised Linux servers after the vulnerabilities used for initial entry have been patched. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry showed GSocket-related detections rising 356.2% between March and August. The activity has particularly affected web applications and hosting environments, which accounted for 87.1% of detected incidents. PHP applications and cPanel hosting represented 63.9% of incidents, while Apache represented 24.3%.

GSocket enables the compromised server and the attacker to each make outbound connections to a relay network, which matches them and creates an encrypted session. This means the compromised host does not need an inbound listener, a public IP address, or a dedicated attacker-controlled command-and-control server, making IP- and domain-based blocking less effective. Attackers have disguised GSocket as kernel threads and used cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files to remain on systems; some also attempted to exploit the Dirty Frag flaw, CVE-2026-43284, to gain root privileges. Microsoft recommends removing GSocket-related files, verifying that relay connections have stopped, restricting outbound traffic, auditing persistence locations, and keeping operating systems and applications patched.

  • GSocket can let an attacker reconnect without knowing the compromised server’s IP address or hostname, reducing the usefulness of IP- and domain-based blocking lists.
  • Because both sides initiate outbound connections, traditional inbound firewall rules may not detect this activity; the article specifically points to egress filtering and outbound monitoring as more relevant controls.
  • Attackers were observed disguising GSocket as kernel threads and establishing persistence through cron jobs, systemd services, and shell startup files, giving defenders concrete locations to audit.
  • Some attackers attempted to use CVE-2026-43284, known as Dirty Frag, to obtain root-level control on affected Linux hosts.

Attackers are using a legitimate remote-access program called GSocket to keep returning to Linux servers after breaking into them, even when the original security weakness has been fixed. The activity mainly affects web applications and web-hosting systems, especially PHP sites, cPanel hosting, and Apache servers, with education and research organizations among the most common targets. It matters because the tool lets attackers communicate through outgoing internet connections, making them harder to block with the usual protections that stop unsolicited incoming connections.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

The article reports active, increasing abuse of GSocket for persistent access to Linux servers, particularly web and hosting environments. It provides concrete detection trends, affected technologies, persistence methods, and defensive actions relevant to many security teams.

The Apache Software Foundation has patched CVE-2026-119618, a critical flaw in the mod_http2 component of Apache HTTP Server. The issue is a race condition in assign_headers() that can corrupt heap memory when shared resources are used by concurrent threads without proper synchronization. An unauthenticated attacker could potentially use this corruption to run code with the web server process’s privileges.

Affected versions include Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42, provided HTTP/2 is enabled. Wiz reported that 64% of cloud environments have vulnerable resources and roughly half have publicly exposed instances, although that estimate does not account for HTTP/2 being disabled by default. Wiz said it knew of no public exploits or attacks at the time of publication, while watchTowr recommended patching immediately or disabling HTTP/2 until patching is possible.

  • The reported exposure figures may overstate immediate risk because the affected HTTP/2 feature is disabled by default and must be enabled for the flaw to be reachable.
  • Administrators that cannot patch immediately can reduce risk by disabling HTTP/2, an interim measure specifically recommended by watchTowr.
  • Successful exploitation would run commands with the web server process's privileges, meaning the impact depends on what access that process has on the host.
  • Although no public exploit or active attacks were known at publication, Wiz warned that this could change soon.

Apache has fixed a serious flaw in its widely used website-serving software that could let an outsider take control of a vulnerable server without logging in. The issue affects certain recent Apache versions when their newer web connection feature is turned on, and cloud-security data suggests many organizations may have affected systems exposed to the internet. Because Apache helps run about one in five websites, a successful break-in could let criminals run commands on a website’s server and potentially disrupt or misuse it.

Microsoft has confirmed that Windows updates released since the October 2026 Patch Tuesday are causing SQL Server performance and stability problems. After the queries finish, some connections remain open instead of closing, causing the number of open connections to grow over time and degrade server performance.

The issue affects Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2012 and later. Administrators may be able to temporarily improve stability by manually closing leftover connections or restarting the SQL service, but either action can end active queries and the problem can return. Bitdefender investigated a credential-theft campaign in which attackers abused the legitimate Goddess of Victory: NIKKE game launcher’s server-pushed task channel. The launcher was instructed at runtime to download a malicious file from analytics.insightjs[.]com, without attackers patching the launcher binary, exploiting a vulnerability, or placing malicious content in the shipped game files. The downloaded file was presented as an ordinary launcher log but contained compiled LuaJIT code for an information stealer Bitdefender calls k2f-agent.

The payload ran inside the signed launcher process, used the launcher’s browser-to-native service mechanism, and could collect saved browser credentials, cookies, cryptocurrency-wallet extension data, and developer-related secrets. It could decrypt Chrome password data including data protected by Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption, and it targeted MetaMask, Phantom, Coinbase Wallet, Keplr, and TronLink. Stolen information was sent through the launcher’s existing encrypted telemetry traffic, and the observed download, collection, exfiltration, and cleanup sequence took less than ten minutes; the malicious delivery server has since been taken down.

  • The malware’s ability to handle Chrome’s newer App-Bound Encryption shows it was designed to obtain browser credentials from recent Chrome versions rather than only relying on older password-storage methods.

Since mid-August 2026, Material Security tracked a phishing campaign targeting corporate Google users through Calendar invites and, later, Google Drive file and document-share invitations. The messages used mundane themes such as voicemail notices, payment issues, court summonses, and RFP requests, often sent from compromised accounts belonging to organizations recipients already knew. The campaign used trusted Google redirect links, share.google, Drive links, and in one case Intuit notification links, making the visible domains and certificates appear legitimate.

After a victim clicked through, the Nyasher framework placed a live reverse proxy in front of Google’s genuine sign-in flow and captured the victim’s active session while passing passwords and additional sign-in prompts to Google in real time. Material Security said this approach could capture sessions despite SMS codes, authenticator codes, Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based recovery, potentially giving an attacker access to mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name. During one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers blocked 68,676 campaign messages, analyzed 2,112 malicious URLs, took down 897 domains, and identified 8,570 compromised sender addresses; reported phishing destinations were placed behind Cloudflare warning pages.

  • Stopping a stolen live session requires rapid response: teams may need to revoke sessions, remove OAuth permissions, and reset accounts within an hour to limit access to mail and Drive.

Researchers found a scam that sent fake Google Calendar and Drive invitations from email accounts people already trusted, using ordinary-looking subjects such as payment notices or document requests. Clicking the links could lead victims to a convincing Google sign-in page that let criminals take over an already approved account session, even after the victim completed the usual extra login check. Corporate Google users are affected because a stolen session can give an intruder access to email, files, and permissions to connect other apps. The campaign shows that trusted links and familiar senders can still be used to deceive people, while attackers can cheaply replace blocked websites and try again.

New SignDrop Zero-Day Exploit Turns Windows CLFS Security Feature Into SYSTEM Access

Public SignDrop proof-of-concept code claims a local Windows user can abuse the CLFS log-authentication feature and Microsoft Defender to gain SYSTEM privileges on recent Windows versions. Microsoft has not confirmed, assigned a CVE, or patched the issue, though independent testing found the exploit works but is unreliable and conspicuous.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A public proof of concept named SignDrop claims that a local Windows user can gain SYSTEM privileges by abusing companion-file creation in the Common Log File System driver’s log-authentication feature.
  • 02The published exploit redirects creation of a CLFS .cnpf recovery file through object manager symbolic links and uses the Microsoft Defender antimalware service as the privileged process in its demonstrated chain.
  • 03The researcher says recent Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025 systems are affected when the CLFS Authentication Mode registry setting is 0 or 1, while modes 2 and 3 disable the mitigation but allow CLFS to parse tampered log files.
  • 04Researcher Heewon Song of 78researchlab independently tested the exploit and found it works, but assessed that it is not reliable enough for operational use.
  • 05Microsoft had not confirmed SignDrop, assigned it a CVE, or released a patch as of the article’s publication.

Public proof-of-concept code called SignDrop claims that a local Windows user can obtain SYSTEM privileges through the Common Log File System (CLFS) driver. The technique targets a log-authentication feature Microsoft added in October 2025 to protect CLFS log files from tampering. Microsoft had not confirmed the flaw, assigned it a CVE, or released a fix at the time of publication.

According to the researcher, an attacker can prepare a CLFS log and use object manager symbolic links to redirect creation of a related .cnpf recovery file when a privileged process opens the log. The published chain uses the Microsoft Defender antimalware service, causing the file to be created under SYSTEM privileges while remaining writable by the standard user, which can be chained into a SYSTEM shell. Independent testing by 78researchlab found the exploit works but is not reliable enough for operational use, and the demonstrated method is noticeable because it alters UAC prompts to open both standard-user and SYSTEM shells.

  • The CLFS authentication protection intended to prevent tampered log files from being parsed is itself the feature SignDrop targets, through creation of its associated recovery file.
  • The claimed affected configuration includes both learning and enforced authentication modes, and established systems typically move automatically to enforced mode after 90 days.
  • Disabling CLFS authentication removes the claimed SignDrop attack surface but re-enables the risk that CLFS will parse tampered log files, which the protection was designed to prevent.
  • The published demonstration depends on Microsoft Defender being enabled and visibly causes UAC prompts to open both a standard-user shell and a SYSTEM shell, making the activity noticeable to someone using the computer.

A researcher released code claiming that an ordinary Windows user can take full control of a computer by abusing a part of Windows that manages system logs, with Microsoft Defender used in the demonstrated method. The claimed issue affects recent Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025 systems using the default log-protection settings, and independent testing found that it can work, though not reliably. This matters because full system control could let someone bypass normal limits on an account, while turning off the affected protection could expose computers to older, more serious flaws. Microsoft has not yet confirmed the issue or issued a fix.

Critical Red Hat Quay Flaw Lets Attackers Read and Overwrite All Private Container Images in a Registry

Red Hat has patched two critical Quay flaws that could let unauthenticated or low-privilege attackers steal and overwrite private container images across registry tenants. Organizations should urgently install fixed Quay releases, restrict access to the /keys endpoint, and rotate potentially exposed robot credentials.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-123710 is a critical Red Hat Quay flaw with a CVSS score of 9.8 that can allow attackers to add a trusted signing key and create tokens for any repository.
  • 02When anonymous access is enabled, CVE-2026-123710 can be exploited without an account, while disabling anonymous access still leaves the flaw exploitable by any valid Quay user.
  • 03Attackers exploiting CVE-2026-123710 can read private images, obtain secrets or credentials stored in them, overwrite images, and disrupt normal registry access by deleting active signing keys.
  • 04CVE-2026-110697, rated 9.9, can allow Quay users who create specially named namespaces to obtain other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to access or modify their images.
  • 05Red Hat released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches and recommends blocking untrusted access to the /keys endpoint, reviewing relevant audit events, removing unrecognized service keys, and updating Quay.

Red Hat disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in Red Hat Quay, a container-image registry, and released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches. CVE-2026-123710, rated 9.8, can let an attacker add an attacker-controlled signing key that Quay will trust for tokens granting access to any repository. If anonymous access is enabled, no account is needed; if it is disabled, any valid Quay account can still exploit the issue. Attackers could read private images and secrets within them, overwrite images that downstream systems later pull, or delete active keys and cause normal pushes and pulls to fail.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-110697, has a CVSS score of 9.9 and can allow a Quay user who can create a namespace to obtain other tenants’ robot-account tokens. The issue occurs because an underscore in a namespace name acts as a wildcard in an SQL search, potentially returning another tenant’s robot accounts and decrypted tokens. Red Hat says the stolen credentials can be used to read, push, or overwrite images, including potentially injecting malicious images into OpenShift CI/CD pipelines. The company recommends installing the fixed releases, blocking untrusted access to the /keys endpoint, reviewing audit logs for suspicious key events, removing unknown service keys, and rotating affected robot tokens.

  • Disabling anonymous access is not sufficient protection for CVE-2026-123710, because any authenticated Quay user can still obtain a usable token and exploit the key-handling weakness.
  • Removing an unauthorized signing key before applying the update is only temporary, since an attacker can add another key through the same vulnerable endpoint.
  • A planted signing key can persist through restarts and remain valid after password resets or robot-token changes, making post-incident cleanup dependent on identifying and removing unrecognized keys.
  • The second flaw stems from an underscore being treated as a wildcard in a database search, allowing a specially named namespace to match another tenant’s robot accounts and expose decrypted tokens.
  • Red Hat advises limiting creation of namespaces containing underscores and rotating tokens for matching namespaces until updates are deployed, but states that only updating fully resolves CVE-2026-110697.

Red Hat disclosed and fixed two severe problems in its Quay software, which companies use to store and distribute the packaged software needed to run applications. One flaw can let anyone who can reach a Quay registry—sometimes without even creating an account—view private software packages or replace them with harmful versions; the other can let a user steal other customers’ automated access credentials. This matters because altered software packages can spread to every system that later downloads them, potentially exposing secrets and inserting malicious code into company development and delivery processes.

The issues affect all Quay 3 and Quay 5 versions and can impact OpenShift-integrated registries and CI/CD pipelines, making prompt remediation highly important.

The issues include multiple critical NetScaler memory overflow and memory corruption bugs with CVSS scores ranging from 9.3 to 9.5. Depending on the affected configuration, these bugs can cause unpredictable behavior or denial of service. Citrix said it is not aware of exploitation of the disclosed vulnerabilities.

  • The Secure Access Client issues require an existing low-privileged local user, but could elevate that user to SYSTEM on Windows or root on Linux.
  • Citrix said the fixes resulted from a deeper codebase review using AI-assisted code analysis, rather than from known active exploitation.

Citrix released fixes for 12 serious security problems in its NetScaler networking products and its Secure Access Client software for Windows and Linux. MongoDB CVE-2026-118383 is a critical pre-authentication use-after-free flaw that can crash a vulnerable lagging replica-set member if it later becomes primary. KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-118383 is a MongoDB Server use-after-free flaw that can be triggered by two unauthenticated ping requests containing readConcern.afterOpTime values.

  • 03MongoDB rated the flaw 9.5 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0 and released fixed versions for affected branches, while stating it was not aware of exploitation attempts.

  • 05MongoDB Atlas clusters will receive fixes during maintenance, while self-managed users should upgrade every replica-set member and restrict database network access until upgrades are complete.

MongoDB released fixes for CVE-2026-118383, a critical use-after-free flaw rated 9.5 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. Datadog Security Labs reported that an unauthenticated client can send two specially crafted ping requests to a vulnerable replica-set member, even when authentication is enabled. The member does not immediately crash; the failure requires it to later be elected as the main server while it is missing recent changes. MongoDB said it was not aware of attempts to exploit the issue.

The flaw occurs during the elected member’s catch-up process, when cleanup can run twice and reuse memory that has already been freed, causing a crash before the new main server accepts writes. It affects replica-set members, including shard and configuration server members in sharded clusters, but not a standalone MongoDB server. MongoDB Atlas clusters will receive fixed versions during maintenance, while self-managed deployments need to upgrade every replica-set member and verify versions on containers and previously offline members. Until upgrades are complete, researchers recommend limiting database network access to only required systems, though this does not eliminate the flaw.

  • Enabling authentication alone does not stop the two malicious requests on vulnerable versions, even though the requests can be sent by a client without credentials.
  • The planted request state can remain on a server until it restarts, rolls back changes, or stops being the primary server, meaning the triggering requests may occur well before a later failover.
  • An attacker cannot directly make the targeted server fall behind, win the election, or determine when those conditions occur, which limits their control over when a crash happens.
  • Administrators can investigate suspected activity by correlating unauthenticated slow ping queries with two catch-up exit log events and a subsequent crash involving CatchupState::abort_inlock().
  • MongoDB 8.2 is no longer supported and is absent from the affected-version list, but a published proof of concept reported the issue in a lab test of version 8.2.12 using a test-only setting.

MongoDB has fixed a serious flaw that lets someone without an account send two specially made requests that can later crash a database server under certain failover conditions. It affects MongoDB installations that use groups of servers to keep backup copies of the same data, including some larger sharded setups, but not a single standalone server. A crash can leave a service without its main database server and disrupt normal operations, so customers running their own systems should install the fixed version on every server in the group; MongoDB’s hosted Atlas service will receive updates during maintenance.

A critical flaw, CVE-2026-119618, in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 component, mod_http2, can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. It affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when HTTP/2 is enabled and is fixed in version 2.4.71. Red Hat assigned a CVSS score of 9.8 and said an attacker could take full control of the server process.

HTTP/2 is enabled through the Apache Protocols directive, either across a server or for individual virtual hosts, using h2 for encrypted connections and h2c for unencrypted connections. Administrators should upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71; those unable to update can remove h2 and h2c and leave Protocols http/1.1 as a temporary measure. Red Hat released fixes for RHEL 9 and 10, while RHEL 6, 7, and 8 are not affected; standalone mod_h2 versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 are affected and currently have no fixed release.

  • HTTP/2 may be enabled either for an entire Apache server or for individual virtual hosts, so checking only a global setting may miss affected sites.
  • Red Hat considers the issue less severe on RHEL 9 and 10 because its mod_http2 packages use a separate memory allocator for each HTTP/2 connection stream, which the vendor says makes exploitation much harder.
  • The standalone mod_h2 project has no fixed release, and its archived repository’s latest release, 2.0.42, is still affected; disabling HTTP/2 is the stated option for those deployments.
  • There is conflicting public information about exploit availability: Red Hat says public research demonstrated a reliable exploit, while Wiz reported that no exploit was available and found no reported in-the-wild exploitation.
  • Updating to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.67 or any later release through 2.4.70 does not address this newly reported flaw; the article identifies 2.4.71 as the fixed upstream release.

A serious bug in Apache HTTP Server can let an outsider take control of a website’s server without needing a password when the server uses its newer HTTP/2 connection option. It affects Apache versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, as well as some separate mod_h2 builds, but only where HTTP/2 has been turned on. Organizations running affected servers should install the fixed version or temporarily turn off HTTP/2, because a successful break-in could give an attacker control of the server process.

An attacker used 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 repositories and deploy a CI credential-stealing payload that executed in at least 1,806, exposing repository secrets and cloud credentials.   • 03SafeDep identified malicious commits in 8,093 public repositories, including 7,309 where the stealer was inserted into an existing workflow and 771 where it was delivered through an npm postinstall hook.

An attacker used stolen credentials from 4,837 GitHub accounts to test write access in 61,764 repositories through pull requests titled docs: dependency audit notes from wfx-docs branches. Aikido Security reported that a CI secret-stealing payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories, while SafeDep identified malicious commits in 8,093 public repositories. The attacker usually reverted the malicious changes within minutes and often deleted workflow logs or entire runs.

The payload was designed to collect GitHub Actions secrets, workflow tokens, cloud credentials, credential files, repository data, and recent workflow artifacts. In some cases it was inserted as an npm postinstall hook, meaning it could also run on a developer’s machine during npm install. It could use GitHub identity tokens to access AWS, GCP, and Azure environments and establish persistence by changing AWS role trust policies or adding Azure federated credentials. Repository owners are advised to revoke compromised account access, enable 2FA, rotate all accessible secrets and variables, and check cloud environments for the listed persistence indicators.

  • A repository should treat any account that opened the attacker's test pull request as compromised, even when no payload was subsequently observed.
  • The absence of visible artifacts such as wfx-loot files, cache entries, or workflow summaries does not rule out data theft; a missing run number on the attacker's commit is described as a more reliable sign that the payload executed.
  • Credential rotation alone may not remove access because the payload can alter AWS role trust policies and create Azure federated credentials that let repository workflows sign in without stored secrets.
  • The incident extended beyond repository workflows: an npm postinstall hook could execute on a developer's machine, and a malicious Packagist release could trigger it when npm install was run inside its vendor directory.

Someone used login details stolen from 4,837 GitHub accounts to add hidden code to software projects that could collect passwords, cloud-account access details, and other sensitive information. The activity reached thousands of projects, including projects where the stolen accounts had permission to make changes for other people or organizations. This matters because the stolen information could let the attacker enter connected online services, keep access even after some passwords are changed, and potentially affect software packages used by others.

Node.js released security updates for supported 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines fixing 16 flaws, including HTTP/2 and HTTPS bugs that can crash servers, leak memory or other connections’ data, and potentially expose TLS private keys. Organizations running Node.js servers should upgrade to 22.23.5, 24.22.3, or 26.13.1 immediately, as no workarounds are listed and end-of-life versions remain vulnerable.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Node.js released versions 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1 to address 16 vulnerabilities, seven of which are rated high severity.
  • 02CVE-2026-123863 can allow an unauthenticated client to crash default Node.js HTTP/2 servers on the 24.x and 26.x release lines when the server responds before the request body fully arrives.
  • 03CVE-2026-123866 can cause a Node.js HTTP/2 server to send a client portions of memory that may include responses intended for other connections, and it affects all three supported release lines.
  • 04CVE-2026-123864 affects Node.js HTTPS servers and can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, including TLS private keys and other users' requests, under specific handler conditions.

Node.js released versions 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1 to fix 16 vulnerabilities, including seven rated high severity. The issues affect the runtime’s built-in HTTP/2, HTTPS, and TLS server code, making them relevant where a Node.js process directly accepts those connections. Node.js lists updating as the only fix and provides no workaround for servers that cannot update.

CVE-2026-123863 can let an unauthenticated client crash default HTTP/2 servers on 24.x and 26.x when a response is sent before the full request body arrives, which the project describes as typical behavior. CVE-2026-123866 can cause HTTP/2 servers on all supported lines to send clients pieces of memory, including responses intended for other connections. A separate HTTPS flaw, CVE-2026-123864, can expose memory from other connections, including TLS private keys and other users’ requests, under specific handler conditions. End-of-life Node.js versions, including 20.x and 25.x, receive no fix and are always affected, while the advisory reports no known exploitation.

  • The HTTP/2 crash flaw CVE-2026-123863 can affect typical server behavior because it requires only that a server respond before the full request body arrives, and it works over both encrypted and unencrypted connections.
  • The HTTPS memory-disclosure flaw CVE-2026-123864 applies only to handlers that send headers early with res.flushHeaders() and later finish with data, but leaked memory can include TLS private keys and other users' requests if a route also returns or stores request bodies.
  • Node.js HTTP/2 file-serving endpoints using stream.respondWithFile() or stream.respondWithFD() have distinct risks: memory corruption on 24.x and 26.x and server crashes from canceled downloads on all supported lines.
  • A TLS 1.2 renegotiation issue can let a client accepted for one hostname change to another hostname with stricter client-certificate requirements without satisfying those stricter rules.
  • The advisory reports no known attacks, but it offers no workaround for servers that cannot update and leaves end-of-life Node.js lines, including 20.x and 25.x, without fixes.

Node.js released updates to fix 16 security problems, including bugs that could let an unauthenticated person crash websites or services built with its built-in web connection features. Some flaws could expose pieces of a server’s memory, potentially revealing other users’ requests or secret website encryption keys. Organizations that run affected Node.js servers should update to versions 22.23.5, 24.22.3, or 26.13.1, because older unsupported versions will not receive fixes.

  • 01Google Cloud warned that three AMD EPYC Turin CPU flaws could allow code running on the same processor core inside a virtual machine to infer data from other processes or the kernel.
  • 02Google says it has already applied mitigations for attacks between virtual machines and between virtual machines and the host, while affected machine series include C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D, and G4.
  • 03The flaws are TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350), TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), and the newly disclosed CVE-2026-0004, also called TSA-Fill by the Xen Project.

Google Cloud warned that three AMD EPYC Turin processor flaws could allow code running on the same processor core within a virtual machine to infer data from other processes or the kernel. The affected Google Cloud machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D, and G4, including C4D and Z4D bare-metal instances. Google rated the issue Medium and said it has already applied mitigations for attacks between VMs and between VMs and the host. The remaining concern is exposure among processes inside an affected VM.

The flaws are transient scheduler attacks: TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350), TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), and CVE-2026-0004, which the Xen Project calls TSA-Fill. AMD says Zen 5 processors, including Turin, are affected differently than previously characterized AMD processors. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity and low privilege requirements, and neither AMD nor Google reported exploitation. None of the flaws was in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at the time of publication.

For affected VMs, customers should install their operating-system vendor’s fix when available, then stop and start the VM after Google updates the CPU information reported to it; Google states that rebooting the guest OS alone is not enough. Bare-metal customers running their own operating system or hypervisor should apply vendor fixes, while GKE node images for Turin-based bare-metal instances are planned and Cloud Run requires no action. For Turin systems on customer-owned hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed for full mitigation, which may affect performance.

  • For affected Google Cloud VMs, an ordinary reboot is explicitly insufficient; customers must stop and start the VM after Google updates the CPU information it reports.
  • Google has addressed the higher-isolation risks between VMs and between a VM and its host, but processes within the same VM may still be exposed until the guest operating system mitigation is enabled.
  • Customers may face a remediation gap because Google provides no interim action for operating systems whose vendors have not released a fix, and does not explain how to determine when its CPU-information update has reached a VM.
  • As of the article’s publication, none of the three flaws was listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and neither AMD nor Google reported active exploitation.

Google Cloud says three flaws in newer AMD server chips could let someone who is already able to run a program inside a virtual machine learn information from other programs or the operating system on the same chip core. The issue affects Google Cloud C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D, and G4 machines using AMD Turin processors, including certain dedicated physical servers. Google has protected against data exposure between separate customers’ virtual machines, but affected customers need operating-system updates and must fully stop and start their virtual machines when the update is available. The flaws show that shared cloud hardware can create privacy risks even when customers’ systems are meant to be isolated.

  • 01Island identified a TypoPrompting campaign involving 186 lookalike domains across 27 AI brands, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Lovable, and Cursor.

Island researchers identified a campaign called TypoPrompting that uses 186 lookalike domains across 27 AI brands, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek, Perplexity, and Midjourney. The domains target people who mistype familiar AI-service addresses and redirect them to malicious or unwanted destinations. Some listed lookalikes include cloude[.]ai, chatlgpt[.]com, geimini[.]com, deepceek[.]com, and preplexity[.]ai.

The campaign uses three routes: ClickFix-style fake verification pages, fake Security Check pages delivering Net Guard, and Chrome extensions that hijack searches. The ClickFix route fingerprints the browser and collects the public IP address before presenting a fake Cloudflare page that instructs Windows users to run a PowerShell command, macOS users to run a shell command, or visitors to download and run an executable. Island said Net Guard is the unmodified Microsoft Store app signed by Microsoft, but it can run operator-controlled JavaScript, change Chrome’s default search engine while the user is idle, edit browser profiles, and install arbitrary Chrome extensions.

A Perplexity lookalike, preplexity[.]ai, redirects to the Quick Search extension, which changes the browser’s default search provider to find.flashysearches[.]com and sends searches to a third party. Island found Quick Search belongs to a group of 16 Chrome Web Store extensions with 972,000 declared users as of November 3, 2026. The article notes that workplace searches routed this way can include internal hostnames, customer names, and project details.

  • Net Guard is distributed byte-for-byte as the Microsoft Store version and carries Microsoft’s Store signature, yet Island said every copy includes hidden browser-control capabilities that activate without asking.
  • The ClickFix fingerprinting gate extends beyond AI lookalikes to 211 entry domains impersonating banks, insurers, telecoms, and enterprise software providers.
  • Quick Search can redirect searches to a third party through its browser-search-provider setting without needing executable JavaScript or declared permissions for its main action.
  • Some AI lookalike domains, including cloude[.]ai and cluade[.]ai, were registered as early as July 2023, showing that the infrastructure predates the reported campaign by years.

Researchers found 186 web addresses that closely resemble popular AI services such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity, hoping to catch people who make a small typing mistake. These sites can trick visitors into copying and running harmful commands, installing a program that changes browser settings, or adding extensions that redirect searches. This affects everyday users and workplaces because redirected searches may reveal internal company names, customer names, and project details to outside parties.

Apache HTTP Server: Critical RCE Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-119618 )

Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55–2.4.70 with HTTP/2 enabled are affected by critical unauthenticated RCE CVE-2026-119618; upgrade to 2.4.71 immediately or disable mod_http2/HTTP/2 until patched.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-119618 is a critical race condition in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 component that can corrupt memory and potentially allow unauthenticated remote code execution.
  • 02Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and standalone mod_h2 versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 are affected when HTTP/2 is enabled, while servers supporting only HTTP/1.1 are not affected.
  • 03Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 fixes CVE-2026-119618, and administrators should restart httpd after updating so all child processes load the patched module.
  • 04If patching is delayed, organizations can reduce exposure by disabling HTTP/2 or unloading mod_http2, although these measures are not substitutes for updating.
  • 05No exploitation in the wild had been reported at the time of the notice, but public research reproducing the memory corruption was available.

Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-119618, a critical flaw in the HTTP/2 component of Apache HTTP Server. The issue affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and standalone mod_h2 versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 when HTTP/2 is enabled. Apache rates it Critical, while Red Hat assigned a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8. Servers that support only HTTP/1.1 are not affected.

The flaw is a timing problem in mod_http2’s assign_headers() function, where concurrent threads access a shared header table without sufficient synchronization. An unauthenticated remote attacker could corrupt memory and potentially run code on an affected server, while crashes and service disruption are also possible. The article notes that public research reproducing the memory corruption is available, although no exploitation in the wild had been reported at the time of the notice. Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 fixes the issue, and organizations unable to update immediately can reduce exposure by disabling HTTP/2 or unloading mod_http2, then restarting Apache.

  • An Apache installation may remain protected even if it reports an older version number, because Linux distribution packages can include the fix through vendor security updates; administrators should verify patch status against their vendor’s advisory.
  • Checking only a global Apache configuration is insufficient because HTTP/2 can be enabled within individual VirtualHost settings, so every relevant configuration location must be reviewed.
  • The article notes that attacks may resemble normal HTTP/2 traffic and Apache has published no specific indicators, making repeated web-server crashes, segmentation faults, or unexpected processes run by the web-server account especially important warning signs.
  • Organizations that must preserve HTTP/2 for users can reduce exposure by ending HTTP/2 connections at an unaffected load balancer, CDN, or reverse proxy and sending only HTTP/1.1 traffic to Apache.
  • An update alone is not enough until Apache is restarted rather than merely reloaded, because existing child processes need to load the patched module.

Apache disclosed a critical flaw in certain versions of its widely used web server software that can let an unauthenticated person on the internet potentially take control of a server when its newer HTTP/2 connection feature is enabled. It affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, as well as some separately installed HTTP/2 components, including systems and products that bundle this software. A successful break-in could crash websites, expose sensitive data and credentials, or give an attacker access to other systems reachable from the server, so organizations should update to version 2.4.71 or temporarily turn off HTTP/2.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a critical patch advisory for widely deployed Apache HTTP Server software, with a CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated remote-code-execution risk on affected HTTP/2-enabled systems. Security professionals should prioritize identifying exposed instances and applying the Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 update or disabling HTTP/2 if patching is delayed.

A fake legal warning was sent to a hotel reservations mailbox using a legitimate app platform’s own email service, making the message appear trustworthy even though it was not. Transcending the trust boundaries: how a cloud pentest works

Effective cloud pentesting focuses on proving whether attackers can cross trust boundaries between tenant workloads, provider-managed services, control planes, and underlying infrastructure—not merely finding code execution or open ports. Tests should safely verify real cross-tenant or provider-level impact through minimal, authorized actions.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cloud penetration testing should assess whether attackers can cross trust boundaries between tenant resources, provider-managed services, internal provider components, and underlying infrastructure rather than merely identify open ports or achieve code execution.
  • 02The article models cloud platforms in three layers: the public External layer, the provider’s logical Overlay layer for service runtimes and internal components, and the physical and virtualization-focused Underlay layer.
  • 03A confirmed trust-boundary violation requires more than seeing or authenticating to an internal service; the tester must obtain authorization and safely perform a controlled action outside the original boundary.
  • 04Service account credentials, network access, and runtime context must be evaluated together because an over-privileged credential can enable access to internal APIs even when network segmentation is strict.
  • 05Cloud pentests of provider infrastructure require separate authorization and should confirm cross-tenant effects only with controlled test tenants and synthetic data.

This article presents a methodology for penetration testing cloud platforms by examining the trust boundaries between customer resources, provider-managed services, internal provider components, and the underlying infrastructure. It argues that finding remote code execution or an open port is not sufficient to measure cloud risk. The meaningful result is whether a tester can demonstrate a controlled transition into a more trusted zone, such as another tenant’s resources or a provider management component.

The methodology divides a cloud into an External layer, an Overlay layer for service runtimes and provider components, and an Underlay infrastructure layer containing hosts, hypervisors, networks, and storage. Testers should evaluate network visibility together with the credentials and permissions available in the current environment, especially service account tokens that may be accepted by internal APIs. Confirmed impact requires more than reaching or authenticating to an internal service: the tester must receive authorization and perform a minimal, safe action beyond the original trust boundary, preferably using controlled test tenants and synthetic data.

  • A managed service with the same customer-facing name can have radically different security boundaries depending on whether it runs in a dedicated virtual machine, a shared Kubernetes cluster, or another provider-specific design.
  • Remote code execution inside a tenant container or service runtime may only establish an initial foothold; the critical question is whether it yields credentials, internal access, or permissions that reach other tenants or provider systems.
  • An internal service being reachable over the network is not proof of compromise, because some clouds intentionally expose internal services while still requiring valid service credentials or certificates.
  • A stolen service account token is only useful if the tester identifies who issued it, which systems accept it, what tenant it is tied to, and what actions it authorizes.
  • A failed attempt to move beyond a tenant environment is still valuable evidence because it can show that a trust boundary is enforced by real controls rather than assumed to be secure.

The article explains how security testers examine cloud services by checking whether a customer can get past the barriers that should separate their own account and data from other customers and the cloud provider’s internal systems. It matters to cloud customers and providers because a flaw in a shared service, login credential, backup system, or virtual machine could let an attacker access another customer’s data or disrupt systems used by many people. The safest tests use provider permission and controlled test accounts, proving only the smallest necessary action rather than touching real users’ information.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-119618) Apache HTTP Server Remote Code Execution via mod_http2

Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55–2.4.70 with mod_http2 and HTTP/2 enabled are vulnerable to pre-authentication remote code execution via CVE-2026-119618; upgrade to 2.4.71 or later or disable h2/h2c until patched.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-119618 is a critical race condition in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 that can corrupt memory and may allow remote code execution without authentication.
  • 02Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are affected when mod_http2 is loaded and HTTP/2 is enabled through the Protocols directive.
  • 03Apache fixed the issue in version 2.4.71, released on November 11, 2026.
  • 04The article states that the vulnerability is not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and that there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.
  • 05Until patching is confirmed, defenders should identify exposed Apache servers, check whether h2 or h2c is enabled, and disable HTTP/2 where it is not needed.

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical race condition in Apache HTTP Server’s mod_http2 component that can corrupt memory in a server child process and may enable remote code execution. An attacker needs only network access to a server that accepts HTTP/2 connections, with no authentication or user interaction required. The issue affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when mod_http2 is loaded and HTTP/2 is enabled through the Protocols directive. The article states that there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild and that the flaw is not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Affected systems include public web servers, reverse proxies, and load-balancing tiers that run Apache with HTTP/2 enabled, including potentially overlooked bundled builds in appliances and base images. Apache fixed the vulnerability in version 2.4.71, released on November 11, 2026, though organizations using operating-system packages or vendor-bundled builds should confirm that fixes have been backported. Until patching is confirmed, defenders should inventory internet-facing Apache servers, identify h2 or h2c configurations, disable HTTP/2 where it is not required, and monitor logs for repeated child-process crashes or segmentation faults. The article also recommends disabling cleartext h2c on servers exposed to untrusted networks.

  • External exposure identification is imperfect because most observed systems were identified by service fingerprint rather than confirmed version detection, and HTTP/2 enablement cannot always be verified from outside the server.
  • The risk can be overlooked because affected Apache servers often operate as front-end layers for applications owned by other teams, while appliances and infrequently rebuilt base images may contain bundled Apache versions.
  • Disabling cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c) on systems exposed to untrusted networks is a specific interim measure while patch availability is confirmed.
  • Repeated child-process crashes or segmentation faults in Apache error logs may help defenders identify signs consistent with the memory-corruption issue.
  • Organizations using operating-system packages or vendor-bundled Apache builds should verify vendor backports directly, since package availability and fixed standalone mod_h2 releases were not uniformly confirmed.

The article warns that many Apache web servers may have a serious flaw that could let someone on the internet take control of a server before logging in. It affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when its faster web connection feature, HTTP/2, is turned on, including servers used for public websites, reverse proxies, and traffic-handling systems. Because these systems often sit in front of important applications and are widely used across many industries, organizations should update to version 2.4.71 or later or turn off HTTP/2 until they can patch.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a critical, pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerability affecting widely deployed Apache HTTP Server installations with HTTP/2 enabled. Although no public exploitation has been reported, affected internet-facing web servers, reverse proxies, and load-balancing tiers should be identified and patched or mitigated promptly.

CVE-2026-126187: React Server Components Flaw Lets Attackers Execute Code Through Smuggled Flight Rows

React Server Components packages before 19.0.9, 19.1.10, 19.2.9, and 19.3.1 reportedly contain a critical Flight transport framing flaw that can enable unauthenticated server-side code execution under specific shared-ArrayBuffer conditions. Upgrade affected React/framework dependencies, rebuild and redeploy, and avoid sending multiple typed-array views over a shared ArrayBuffer until patched.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-126187 is described as a critical, unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in React Server Components, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.5.
  • 02The affected packages are react-server-dom-webpack, react-server-dom-parcel, and react-server-dom-turbopack in versions through 19.0.8, 19.1.9, 19.2.8, and 19.3.0.
  • 03The issue requires a response containing multiple typed-array views over a shared ArrayBuffer, attacker-influenced bytes in one view, and a downstream path that transfers the backing storage.
  • 04React fixed the issue in versions 19.0.9, 19.1.10, 19.2.9, and 19.3.1 by copying large typed-array payloads into exact-size buffers before sending them.
  • 05Organizations should upgrade framework-managed or direct dependencies, confirm the resolved package versions in lockfiles, and rebuild and redeploy affected applications.

React published CVE-2026-126187 on November 10, 2026, describing a critical unauthenticated remote code execution issue in React Server Components with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.5. The affected packages are react-server-dom-webpack, react-server-dom-parcel, and react-server-dom-turbopack across specified React 19 release lines. The issue can affect server-side and edge rendering environments, while client-only React applications without a server and applications without an RSC-capable framework or bundler plugin are not affected.

The flaw occurs when a response carries multiple typed-array views over a shared ArrayBuffer, attacker-controlled bytes are present in one view, and a downstream consumer transfers the backing storage. In vulnerable versions, a binary row’s length header can be sent while its payload is silently skipped, allowing the Flight parser to consume later bytes incorrectly and potentially interpret attacker-controlled data as a module-loading row. React fixed the issue in versions 19.0.9, 19.1.10, 19.2.9, and 19.3.1 by copying large typed-array payloads into exact-size buffers before they cross the destination boundary. Organizations should upgrade their framework or direct dependencies, verify resolved versions in lockfiles, rebuild and redeploy affected applications, and avoid transporting multiple shared-buffer views in RSC payloads until updated.

  • The patched Flight parser can still process a deliberately corrupted stream, so the fix depends primarily on the writer no longer emitting a binary-row header without its promised bytes.
  • The vulnerable behavior can occur silently: a transferred or detached shared buffer may cause the writer to retain the binary length header while skipping the now-zero-length payload, without surfacing an error.
  • A smuggled module row can turn data into executable code because a framing mismatch causes the parser to consume later rows as binary data and then resume parsing inside attacker-controlled bytes.
  • Many organizations may not see the affected packages declared directly because they are commonly installed transitively through RSC frameworks, making resolved lockfile versions more important than declared dependencies.
  • A practical stopgap before upgrading is to copy shared typed-array views, such as with sharedView.slice(), before placing them in an RSC payload.

The article describes a critical flaw in parts of React used by websites that build pages on a server before sending them to visitors. Under unusual conditions involving shared chunks of data, an attacker could manipulate a server response so that the server runs code from the website’s own software bundle. Websites using affected React Server Components tools, often through frameworks such as Next.js, need updated versions; browser-only React apps without a server are not affected. The stakes are high because successful abuse could let an unauthenticated outsider run code on a server, so organizations should update and redeploy affected applications.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a technical analysis of a specific critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in widely used React Server Components packages, with fixed releases available. Security professionals supporting React, Next.js, or other RSC deployments should promptly verify resolved dependency versions, upgrade, rebuild, and redeploy affected applications.

Beginning November 10, 2026, attackers used stolen GitHub tokens to place a CI secret-stealing script called WFX in repositories where the compromised accounts had write access. They first opened harmless probe pull requests titled docs: dependency audit notes, then injected the payload through existing GitHub Actions workflows, ordinary shell scripts already run by CI, new workflows, or hidden .ci-*.sh files invoked through npm scripts. The attackers commonly reverted the malicious commit and deleted the related workflow run within minutes, leaving missing run numbers in the GitHub Actions history. GitHub search showed more than 63,000 probe pull requests as of November 12, although the article says the payload reached thousands rather than all probed repositories.

WFX collects GitHub Actions secrets and variables, runner memory, cloud credentials, process environments, credential files, and repository data, then attempts to use cloud sign-in access to reach AWS, GCP, and Azure resources. It also includes persistence attempts such as creating AWS access keys, opening AWS role trust policies to all AWS principals, and adding Azure federated identity credentials named wfx-ci-*. Earlier samples sent data to three IP-based collection servers, while newer samples sent stolen data only to a Telegram chat, making IP blocklists insufficient on their own. The article advises affected organizations to identify suspicious commits and missing workflow runs, rotate all credentials accessible to impacted jobs, remove cloud persistence, and revoke compromised GitHub account access.

  • Blocking the campaign’s known collection IP addresses is insufficient for newer samples, which send stolen archives only to a Telegram chat; an outbound network allowlist is needed to stop both delivery methods.
  • Credential rotation alone may not remove the attacker’s access because WFX attempts to create long-lived AWS access keys, weaken AWS role trust policies, and add Azure federated identity credentials.
  • Bot and automation accounts are particularly high-value targets in this campaign because compromised bot tokens can have write access and may bypass branch-protection controls.

Attackers used stolen GitHub account access to secretly add a data-stealing program to thousands of software projects, then quickly removed the visible changes and erased records of the automated jobs that ran it. The program can collect passwords, secret access keys, and cloud-account credentials from affected projects and sometimes from the computers running their build jobs. This affects project owners, automated bot accounts, software users, and developers who may have installed a compromised project version, because stolen access can be used to enter cloud accounts or publish unsafe software later.
